# Half-depth rigidity and the exact cost of reflection extraction

For n=d=1 and any finite number of integer interval fibers, local depth
one half forces central symmetry of the entire positive-length mixed
measure. More precisely, the mass lost under reflection about any actual
mixed point equals the total variation of its through-point cap profile,
plus one explicit own-fiber imbalance. Consequently extraction of a large
convex subbody whose true integer-base centroid has local gamma_1-depth
is equivalent to the corresponding central-reflection retention bound.
This does not prove the universal half-mass retention inequality.

## 1. Setup and the full cap profile

Let C be a compact convex body in R^2, with coordinates (z,x), and put

    S=C intersect (Z times R), mu=H_1 restricted to S,
    M=mu(S)>0, K_z={x:(z,x) in C}.

There are finitely many nonempty integer fibers, each a compact interval
or a point. Zero-length fibers have zero mu mass and are retained as
geometric sets where needed. Fix any actual point y=(j,c) in S. Write

    w_0=|K_j|,
    U_0=|K_j intersect [c,infinity)|,
    m_+=sum_(k>=1)|K_(j+k)|, m_-=sum_(k>=1)|K_(j-k)|.

Missing intervals and zero-length intervals contribute zero length. Define

    F(a)=mu{(z,x):x-c-a(z-j)>=0},  a in R,            (1)
    R(y)=mu(S intersect (2y-S)).

The function F is continuous, piecewise affine, and constant for all
sufficiently large positive and negative a. Its two limits are

    F(+infinity)=m_-+U_0,
    F(-infinity)=m_++U_0.                            (2)

Every nonvertical through-y boundary meets each positive interval fiber
in at most one point. It therefore has zero mu measure, and the opposite
closed cap has mass exactly M-F(a). The two through-y vertical caps have
masses `m_-+w_0` and `m_++w_0`. These are respectively at least the
two limits in (2), so they cannot lower the infimum over the nonvertical
orientations. Moving any containing cap parallel until its boundary
passes through y does not increase its mass. Consequently the absolute
mixed depth at y is exactly

    A_C(y)=min{inf_a F(a), M-sup_a F(a)}
          =M/2-sup_a |F(a)-M/2|.                    (3)

There is no hidden vertical-boundary loss in this identity.

## 2. Convex nesting gives an exact total-variation identity

For k>=1 define the two slope intervals

    I_k^+=(K_(j+k)-c)/k,
    I_k^-=(c-K_(j-k))/k.                             (4)

A missing fiber gives the empty set. For k<ell, convexity and the actual
point (j,c) imply

    c+(k/ell)(K_(j+ell)-c) subset K_(j+k),
    c+(k/ell)(K_(j-ell)-c) subset K_(j-k).

Thus each family is nested:

    I_1^+ contains I_2^+ contains ...,
    I_1^- contains I_2^- contains ....               (5)

Choose a outside the finitely many endpoints of these intervals. In each
family its active indices form a prefix `{1,...,r_+(a)}` or
`{1,...,r_-(a)}`. Point intervals have no effect away from this finite
exceptional set. Differentiating the elementary interval cap lengths in
(1) gives, almost everywhere,

    F'(a)=sum_(k>=1) k(1_(I_k^-)(a)-1_(I_k^+)(a)).    (6)

Since the two active sets are prefixes, all nonzero indicator differences
at this a have the same sign. Hence

    |F'(a)|=sum_(k>=1) k |1_(I_k^-)(a)-1_(I_k^+)(a)|. (7)

This uses the geometry of the actual convex body, not an arbitrary
collection of intervals or arbitrary log-concave sample weights.

For the reflected pair of fibers j-k,j+k, its original mass minus its
retained mass is

  |K_(j+k)|+|K_(j-k)|
       -2|K_(j+k) intersect (2c-K_(j-k))|
    =k |I_k^+ symmetric_difference I_k^-|.

Integrating (7) and summing gives exactly the reflection loss from all
noncentral fibers. The own interval loses

    w_0-|K_j intersect (2c-K_j)|=|2U_0-w_0|.

This formula holds for c in K_j, including endpoints and zero-length
K_j. Equation (2) rewrites it as
`|F(+infinity)+F(-infinity)-M|`. Therefore

  M-R(y)=Var_R(F)
            +|F(+infinity)+F(-infinity)-M|,          (8)

where `Var_R(F)=integral_R |F'(a)| da` is its full total variation.
Both terms are explicit finite piecewise-affine quantities. Equation
(8) is the exact mass cost of central symmetrization at y.

## 3. Complete half-depth rigidity

The following are equivalent for an actual point y=(j,c):

  (i)  A_C(y)=M/2;
  (ii) F(a)=M/2 for every real a;
  (iii) R(y)=M;
  (iv) mu is invariant under reflection about y.

Equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows from (3); (ii) implies (iii) by
(8). If R(y)=M, the positive-length reflected intersections exhaust mu,
so (iv) follows. Conversely a centrally symmetric finite measure puts
at least half its mass in every closed halfspace containing its center:
the halfspace and its reflected copy cover the whole space. A nonvertical
through-center boundary is mu-null, giving equality and hence (i).

One can read the structure directly from (6): if F is constant, then
the weighted prefix counts `r_+(r_++1)/2` and `r_-(r_-+1)/2` agree almost
everywhere. Strict increase of the triangular numbers forces the same
prefix length. Thus each pair of positive-length intervals in (4)
agrees up to null sets, and closed intervals of positive length that
agree almost everywhere agree exactly. Every positive fiber therefore
has an equally long reflected partner. Equation (2) then forces c to
be the midpoint of the own positive interval.

The conclusion is symmetry of the MIXED MEASURE. Unmatched zero-length
boundary fibers may prevent literal equality `S=2y-S`; they do not
affect any assertion above. Since the measure is finite and symmetric,
its true full ambient centroid is y. No centroid hypothesis was needed
to prove the rigidity.

## 4. A finite-fiber quantitative consequence

Suppose y lies on a positive-length fiber and there are N positive
interval fibers. Put `delta=M/2-A_C(y)>=0`. By (3), all F values lie
in `[M/2-delta,M/2+delta]`. If N>=2, the N-1 noncentral fibers give at
most `2(N-1)` distinct breakpoints. F is constant outside their range,
and on each of at most `2(N-1)-1` intervening intervals it is affine.
Each change in F has absolute value at most 2delta. Thus (8) yields

    M-R(y)<=4(N-1)delta,       N>=2.                 (9)

For N=1, the exact formula is `M-R(y)=2delta`. The bound (9) may be
weak, and no uniform-in-N replacement is claimed. Its purpose is to
quantify explicitly the retained-mass cost at an approximately half-deep
point; the exact invariant is (8).

## 5. Equivalence with large locally Grünbaum-deep convex extraction

Fix any threshold t with 0<t<=M. The following two statements are
equivalent:

  (a) Some actual integer-base point y in S has R(y)>=t.

  (b) Some convex BODY D subset C has mixed mass at least t, its TRUE
      mixed-volume centroid g has integer base, and every closed ambient
      halfspace through g contains at least half of D's mixed mass.

For (b) implies (a), apply Section 3 to D. Its mixed measure is centrally
symmetric about its true centroid g. Its positive-length source is
contained, up to a null set, in `C intersect (2g-C)`, so `R_C(g)>=mu(D)>=t`.

Conversely assume (a), and put `E=C intersect (2y-C)`. This is compact,
convex, centrally symmetric about y, and has mixed mass R(y). If E has
positive-length fibers at two distinct integer bases, it has nonempty
ambient interior: the convex hull of two positive vertical intervals at
distinct bases is two-dimensional. Then E is an actual convex body, and
we may take D=E. Its true mixed centroid is y and its local depth is one
half by symmetry.

The ambient-interior qualification cannot be omitted: when y lies on a
vertical supporting face, E can be just a positive vertical interval.
If E has only one positive-length integer fiber, reflection forces its
base to be j, the base of y. Then `|K_j|>=R(y)>=t`. Choose any
`0<epsilon<1/2` and take the actual slab subbody

    D=C intersect {j-epsilon<=z<=j+epsilon}.

Its only positive integer fiber is the FULL original K_j. It is a
full-dimensional convex body: a point of K_j lies strictly inside the
displayed slab, and points of int(C) approach that point, so int(C)
meets the slab interior. Its mixed mass is |K_j|, and its true centroid
is the midpoint of this single interval at integer base j. That point
has local depth exactly one half. This proves (b) while possibly
retaining more mass than R(y).

In particular, at t=M/2 the proposed large locally-gamma_1-deep extraction
is EXACTLY the universal half-mass central-reflection-retention question
for n=d=1. Neither assertion is proved for arbitrary fiber count here.
This equivalence prevents treating the extraction mechanism as an
independent resolution of the still-unsettled reflection bound.

## 6. Exact checks on the archived four-fiber example

For K_0=[0,2], K_1=[0,6], K_2=[0,10], K_3=[0,3], total M=21,
the point y=(2,3) has `F(-infinity)=10`, `F(+infinity)=15`,
`Var(F)=5`, own imbalance 4, and R=12. Equation (8) gives
`21-12=5+4`. Its exact absolute depth is 6 by (3).

At the point (2,4), the cap profile has range
[7,14], endpoint values 9 and 14, variation 9, own imbalance 2, and
reflection mass 10. Thus `21-10=9+2`. Maximizing reflection mass and
maximizing ordinary depth are distinct even in this elementary body.
The exact verifier is `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_interval_reflection_variation_identity.py`.
